title: What is the difference between `session.timeout.ms`, `heartbeat.interval.ms`, and `max.poll.interval.ms` for detecting a dead consumer — the background heartbeat thread sends heartbeats every `heartbeat.interval.ms` and the broker evicts the consumer if none arrive within `session.timeout.ms` (detects a CRASHED/unreachable consumer), whereas `max.poll.interval.ms` bounds the time between successive `poll()` calls and evicts a consumer that is ALIVE but stuck processing a batch too long (detects a STALLED consumer) — and why does a slow message handler trigger a rebalance via `max.poll.interval.ms` even though heartbeats are still flowing?
shortTitle: What is the difference between session.timeout.ms, heartbeat.interval.ms, and max.poll.interval.ms for detecting a dead consumer?

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka detects a failed consumer two independent ways. A background heartbeat thread sends heartbeats every `heartbeat.interval.ms`, and the group coordinator evicts the consumer if no heartbeat arrives within `session.timeout.ms`, which detects a crashed or network-unreachable consumer. Separately, `max.poll.interval.ms` bounds the time allowed between successive `poll()` calls on the application thread, and the coordinator evicts a consumer that is still alive and heartbeating but stuck processing a batch longer than that interval, which detects a stalled consumer. A slow handler trips the poll interval even while heartbeats flow because heartbeats prove the process is up, while the poll interval proves processing is progressing, and those are different liveness signals on different threads.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a settlement clerk at National Bank of India. The heartbeat is the clerk waving at the supervisor every few seconds to say I am here and alive. The session timeout is the supervisor's rule that if no wave comes for a while, assume the clerk collapsed and reassign their tray. But waving does not prove the clerk is actually clearing slips; the clerk could be frozen staring at one impossible slip while still waving. So there is a second rule, the poll interval: if the clerk does not come back to grab the next handful of slips within a set time, the supervisor assumes they are stuck, even though they keep waving, and reassigns the tray.
s1_definition.oneliner: Heartbeat interval and session timeout detect a dead or unreachable consumer via a background thread, while max poll interval detects a live but stalled consumer via the application thread, so a slow handler triggers a rebalance even with heartbeats still flowing.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kafka detects a failed consumer two independent ways. A background heartbeat thread sends heartbeats every `heartbeat.interval.ms`, and the group coordinator evicts the consumer if no heartbeat arrives within `session.timeout.ms`, which detects a crashed or network-unreachable consumer. Separately, `max.poll.interval.ms` bounds the time allowed between successive `poll()` calls on the application thread, and the coordinator evicts a consumer that is still alive and heartbeating but stuck processing a batch longer than that interval, which detects a stalled consumer. A slow handler trips the poll interval even while heartbeats flow because heartbeats prove the process is up, while the poll interval proves processing is progressing, and those are different liveness signals on different threads.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a settlement clerk at National Bank of India. The heartbeat is the clerk waving at the supervisor every few seconds to say I am here and alive. The session timeout is the supervisor's rule that if no wave comes for a while, assume the clerk collapsed and reassign their tray. But waving does not prove the clerk is actually clearing slips; the clerk could be frozen staring at one impossible slip while still waving. So there is a second rule, the poll interval: if the clerk does not come back to grab the next handful of slips within a set time, the supervisor assumes they are stuck, even though they keep waving, and reassigns the tray.

**One line to remember:** Heartbeat interval and session timeout detect a dead or unreachable consumer via a background thread, while max poll interval detects a live but stalled consumer via the application thread, so a slow handler triggers a rebalance even with heartbeats still flowing.

sections.s2_technical:
Modern Kafka consumers use two separate threads for liveness. A background heartbeat thread handles group membership, and the application thread handles polling and processing. This separation is the key to understanding these three settings, because two of them belong to the heartbeat thread and one belongs to the application thread.

The `heartbeat.interval.ms`, default three seconds, is how often the background thread sends a heartbeat to the group coordinator. Heartbeats are cheap and frequent, and they say the consumer process is alive and connected. You keep this well below the session timeout, commonly a third of it, so several heartbeats fit inside one session window and a single lost heartbeat does not cause eviction.

The `session.timeout.ms`, default forty-five seconds in recent versions, is how long the coordinator waits without a heartbeat before declaring the consumer dead and triggering a rebalance to reassign its partitions. This detects a crashed consumer, a killed process, or a network partition, because in those cases the heartbeat thread stops sending. You set it with `props.put("session.timeout.ms", 45000)`, and it must fall within the broker-allowed range set by group min and max session timeout. A short session timeout detects crashes faster but risks false evictions on brief network blips; a longer one is more tolerant but slower to react.

The `max.poll.interval.ms`, default five minutes, is the maximum time allowed between two successive `poll()` calls on the application thread. Crucially, `poll()` is the signal that the application is making processing progress. If your handler takes longer than this interval to process a batch, the consumer proactively leaves the group, and the coordinator reassigns its partitions. This detects a stalled consumer that is still up and still heartbeating but no longer doing useful work, such as one blocked on a slow downstream call or an infinite loop.

This is exactly why a slow message handler triggers a rebalance even though heartbeats are still flowing. The heartbeat thread keeps running independently, so from the coordinator's membership view the consumer looks alive. But the application thread is stuck inside your handler and has not called `poll()` again within the poll interval, so the poll-interval mechanism concludes that processing has stalled and evicts the consumer. The two mechanisms answer different questions: is the process up, and is the processing progressing.

The practical tuning follows from this. To avoid spurious rebalances from slow processing, you either make the handler faster, reduce `max.poll.records` so each batch is smaller and finishes within the interval, or raise `max.poll.interval.ms` if the work genuinely needs more time. To tune crash detection, you adjust the session timeout and heartbeat interval together, keeping the heartbeat interval a small fraction of the session timeout. A senior nuance is that after a poll-interval eviction, the partitions are reassigned and likely reprocessed, so idempotency matters, and the reprocessing plus the rebalance itself can cascade if many consumers are slow. Another nuance is that doing heavy work on a separate thread and pausing and resuming partitions is a pattern to keep polling while long work proceeds, decoupling processing time from the poll interval.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India runs a settlement consumer that occasionally calls a slow external compliance service per transaction. Operators see frequent rebalances even though the consumers never crash, and they must understand which timeout is firing.

Problem 1 — a consumer whose process dies must be detected and its partitions reassigned. This is exactly what heartbeat interval and session timeout do.

Problem 2 — a consumer that is alive and heartbeating but blocked for minutes on the slow compliance call must also be detected so its work moves elsewhere. This is exactly what max poll interval does.

Problem 3 — operators are confused why a healthy, heartbeating consumer gets evicted. This is exactly the point that heartbeats prove the process is up while the poll interval proves processing is progressing, and they are different signals on different threads.

The code will model a liveness monitor that, given the time since the last heartbeat and the time spent in the current batch, decides whether the coordinator would evict the consumer and why, logged for the settlement group.

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: broker1:9092
    consumer:
      group-id: settlement-service
      properties:
        heartbeat.interval.ms: 3000     # background thread waves every 3s
        session.timeout.ms: 45000       # evict if no wave for 45s (CRASH)
        max.poll.interval.ms: 300000    # evict if no poll() for 5m (STALL)
      max-poll-records: 100
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three liveness snapshots with different heartbeat ages and batch durations, with a session timeout of forty-five seconds and a poll interval of five minutes.

Step 1 — in the healthy case the last heartbeat was one second ago and the batch has run two seconds. Both are well within limits, so the monitor reports a healthy group member and no rebalance.

Step 2 — in the crashed case no heartbeat has arrived for sixty seconds, which exceeds the forty-five-second session timeout. The monitor reports eviction triggered by the session timeout, because the background heartbeat thread stopped, meaning the process is down or unreachable. The coordinator reassigns its partitions.

Step 3 — in the stalled case heartbeats are fine at two seconds, but the application thread has been inside one batch for six minutes, exceeding the five-minute poll interval. The monitor reports eviction triggered by the poll interval, explicitly noting heartbeats were still flowing. This is the subtle case: the process is alive and waving, but processing has stalled, so the poll-interval mechanism evicts it.

```
2026-10-24 23:40:01 [INFO] Healthy consumer → healthy group member
2026-10-24 23:40:01 [WARNING] Crashed/unreachable consumer → EVICTED by session.timeout.ms: no heartbeat for 60000ms (process down/unreachable)
2026-10-24 23:40:01 [WARNING] Alive but stalled on slow compliance call → EVICTED by max.poll.interval.ms: no poll() for 360000ms (handler stalled; heartbeats still OK)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Consumer process
    ├─ Background Heartbeat Thread ──heartbeat every 3s──→ Group Coordinator
    │        │                                                  │
    │        │ (stops only if process down / unreachable)       │ no heartbeat
    │        ▼                                                  │ for session.timeout(45s)?
    │   proves: PROCESS IS UP                                   └──→ EVICT (CRASH detected)
    │
    └─ Application Thread
             │ poll() → process batch → poll() again
             │        │
             │        │ stuck in slow handler (compliance call 6 min)
             │        ▼
             │   no poll() within max.poll.interval(5m)?
             │        └──→ consumer leaves group → EVICT (STALL detected)
             │             (fires EVEN THOUGH heartbeats still flowing)
             ▼
        proves: PROCESSING IS PROGRESSING

  Two independent liveness signals on two threads → two eviction triggers.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka detects a failed consumer in two independent ways, on two different threads, which is the key to these three settings. A background heartbeat thread sends a heartbeat every heartbeat-interval, by default a few seconds, and the group coordinator evicts the consumer if no heartbeat arrives within the session-timeout, by default around forty-five seconds. This mechanism detects a crashed, killed, or network-unreachable consumer, because in those cases the heartbeat thread simply stops sending. I keep the heartbeat interval well below the session timeout, usually about a third, so one lost heartbeat does not cause a false eviction.

The max-poll-interval setting is different because it lives on the application thread. It bounds the time allowed between successive poll calls, and poll is the signal that processing is actually making progress. If my handler takes longer than that interval to process a batch, the consumer proactively leaves the group and its partitions are reassigned. This detects a consumer that is alive and still heartbeating but stalled, for example blocked on a slow downstream call or stuck in a loop.

That is exactly why a slow message handler triggers a rebalance even though heartbeats are still flowing. The heartbeat thread runs independently, so from the coordinator's membership view the process looks alive, but the application thread is stuck inside the handler and has not called poll again within the interval, so the poll-interval mechanism concludes processing has stalled and evicts it. Heartbeats answer is the process up, and the poll interval answers is the processing progressing, and they are separate questions.

In my National Bank of India settlement service, we saw frequent rebalances with no crashes, and the cause was a slow per-transaction compliance call that pushed a batch past the poll interval while heartbeats stayed perfectly healthy. We fixed it by lowering max-poll-records so each batch finished inside the interval, and for the genuinely long work we offloaded it to a worker and used pause and resume so the main thread kept polling. Understanding that heartbeats and the poll interval are two different liveness signals is what let us diagnose it instead of blindly raising timeouts.
